source.datasetName: Credit Card Fraud Detection Training Dataset

provenance.dataGenerationMethod: Real credit card transactions from payment processing network during September 2023. Transactions collected from point-of-sale terminals, online merchants, and ATM networks. Anonymized using k-anonymity (k=10) and differential privacy (ε=2.0).
provenance.dataFormat: CSV with 31 columns: Time (seconds from first transaction), V1-V28 (PCA-transformed features from original transaction data), Amount (transaction value in EUR), Class (0=legitimate, 1=fraud)
provenance.dataSubjectivity: Mixed - transaction amounts and timestamps are objective, but fraud labels represent expert analyst decisions (may include false positives/negatives). Fraud labeling accuracy estimated at 98.5% based on chargeback confirmations.
dataProcessingSteps: Raw transaction extraction from payment processing databases
PII removal: cardholder names, card numbers, merchant identifiers
PCA transformation: 28 principal components derived from original ~60 transaction features (merchant category, location, device fingerprint, etc.)
Differential privacy noise injection: Laplace noise (ε=2.0) added to transaction amounts
Timestamp anonymization: converted to seconds from arbitrary reference point
Geographic generalization: country-level only, no city or merchant location data
k-anonymity enforcement: removed transactions that could uniquely identify patterns (k=10 threshold)
Fraud label verification: cross-referenced with chargeback data and manual analyst reviews

use.intendedUse: Training and evaluation of machine learning models for real-time fraud detection in payment systems. Suitable for research on imbalanced classification, anomaly detection, and cost-sensitive learning. Educational use in financial ML courses.
use.restrictions: Non-commercial research and educational use only. Cannot be used for actual production fraud detection without separate licensing and regulatory approval. Cannot attempt to reverse PCA transformation or re-identify cardholders. Not approved for use outside EU due to GDPR transfer restrictions.
use.legalRightsToUse: Data processing authorized under GDPR Article 6(1)(f) - legitimate interest for fraud prevention. Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) completed. Approved by EU Data Protection Authority. Pseudonymization techniques meet GDPR Article 32 security requirements.
use.privacyMeasures: Multi-layer anonymization: (1) PII removal, (2) PCA transformation prevents feature reversal, (3) k-anonymity (k=10) prevents unique pattern identification, (4) differential privacy (ε=2.0) protects transaction amounts, (5) geographic generalization to country level, (6) temporal anonymization. Re-identification risk assessed at < 0.001% by independent privacy expert.
use.dataProcessingLocation: EU data centers only (Frankfurt, Amsterdam). No cross-border transfers outside EU. Processing infrastructure certified under ISO 27001, PCI-DSS Level 1, and SOC 2 Type II.

_comments.why_this_matters: Financial data is among the most regulated globally (GDPR, PCI-DSS, PSD2, etc.). Comprehensive anonymization documentation is required to demonstrate compliance and enable data sharing for fraud research.
_comments.key_challenges: Balancing data utility with privacy protection - aggressive anonymization reduces model performance. Class imbalance (0.172% fraud) makes this a challenging ML problem. Cannot share raw features due to risk of merchant identification.
_comments.regulatory_context: GDPR requires explicit documentation of anonymization techniques, legal basis, and re-identification risk assessment. PCI-DSS prohibits storage of full card numbers. PSD2 requires strong customer authentication data, which has been removed from this dataset.
_comments.real_world_context: Similar to Kaggle's Credit Card Fraud Detection dataset (from Worldline and ULB). Used by hundreds of researchers but requires careful documentation to demonstrate it's truly anonymized under GDPR.
